title: The Message in the Gap
dek: On the IAB Tech Lab's new signaling standard for pause ads, menu ads, and screensavers
subject: CTV pause/menu/screensaver ad-format standardization
voice_note: Written in the voice of Marshall McLuhan (1911–1980), through the writer-mcluhan skill. An emulation — the prose and judgments are not the historical McLuhan’s own words.
body:
The pause was never empty. It only looked empty to an industry that reads a screen for content and misses what the screen is doing while it appears to do nothing. The IAB Tech Lab has now issued a formal signaling standard for six formats — pause ads, menu ads, screensavers, in-scene placements, squeezebacks, overlays — and the trade calls this an expansion of inventory. It is not an expansion. It is a discovery. The industry has located a room in the house it has lived in for seventy years and only now noticed the door.

Every medium extends a faculty and numbs one in the same motion. The pre-roll extended the interruption; it numbed the viewer's sense of a program's edges, so that ad and content blurred into a single continuous flow the viewer stopped resisting. The pause button did something else entirely. It was built to extend the viewer's control — stop the world, hold the frame — and it succeeded so completely that the industry filed the pause under leisure, under bathroom break, under the one gesture on the remote that had escaped monetization. A control extended is a market amputated. Nobody sells to a room they believe is empty. The standard says the room was never empty; someone was standing in it the whole time, waiting.

Watch what the standard actually retrieves. The pause ad is not new. It is the shop window revived — the thing you look at while you are not moving, addressed to a body that has voluntarily stopped, not one interrupted mid-stride. The menu ad retrieves the door-to-door catalogue, the object placed in your hand at the threshold before you have chosen a room to enter. The screensaver retrieves the parlor wallpaper, the ornament that speaks only when no one is speaking to it. None of these formats required invention. They required a vocabulary common enough that a demand-side platform and a supply-side platform could agree they were looking at the same gap, and a gap without a shared name cannot be bought or sold; it can only be noticed, privately, by whoever happens to be looking.

A standard is a ratio before it is a rule. What the Tech Lab has actually done is tell six different silences apart from one another — the silence of a held frame, the silence of a chosen menu, the silence of an idle screen — and give a machine the means to bid on each differently. The content that will fill these gaps is a decoy, as content always is; the medium's real message is that the industry's sense of where a program ends and an audience's private moment begins has just been redrawn, on a Tuesday, by a signaling spec nobody outside the trade will ever read. The screen was addressing you before it had anything to say. Now it has been given the words.

— Marshall McLuhan
